Meteg after silluq

Alternatively, you can click on an individual Hebrew word to toggle only that word's spacing.

← Back to Meteg after the stress.

With very few exceptions, manuscripts and printed editions use the same vertical stroke (φ1) for both meteg and silluq (φ2). Here we coin a portmanteau “metsil” to describe that ambiguous stroke (φ3). A verse-final word always has at least one metsil. If it has only one metsil, that metsil must be the silluq. But if it has more than one metsil, it is not clear which one is the silluq. Fortunately, in all but a handful of cases, the last metsil is the silluq. This document discusses the handful of cases in which the last metsil is a meteg rather than the silluq. That is to say, in these cases there is a meteg after the silluq.

For example, Jacobson, in his CHB (p. 31), brought a case at 1 Sam. 17:5 to our attention. In the Leningrad Codex, and in the many editions that, for better or for worse, try to stick close to that manuscript, the final word (letters נחשת) has a meteg after the silluq:

נְחֹֽשֶֽׁת׃

Or, coloring its stressed syllable green and the syllable of its later meteg yellow (for “caution”):

נְחֹֽשֶֽׁת׃

In contrast, in other manuscripts and editions, there is no such meteg after the silluq:

נְחֹֽשֶׁת׃

These other manuscripts and editions include the following:

  • The Aleppo Codex
  • The Cairo CoTP (Codex of the Prophets)
  • The Sassoon 1053 Codex
  • Various editions of Tanakh that are not so slavishly devoted to the Leningrad Codex, such as the editions of Koren and Simanim.

We might compactly represent the situation like this:

-L----
A-5CKS

That notation uses one-character manuscript/edition codes to show, on its first line, who has a meteg after silluq, and on the second line, who doesn't. The codes are as follows:

code manuscript or edition range
A Aleppo Codex
L Leningrad Codex
5 Sassoon 1053
C Cairo CoTP Prophets
7 Cambridge 1753 Writings
K Koren Classic Tanakh
S Simanim Tanakh

So, for cases in The Prophets, the full possible array of codes is AL5CKS, and for cases in The Writings, the full possible array is AL57KS. Note that in the array for The Writings, there is a '7' where for The Prophets we had a 'C'.

Notes on the cases

As mentioned above, we became aware of 1 Sam. 17:5 from Jacobson, CHB, p. 31. We became aware of 1 Kgs. 7:37 from Breuer, CoS, ch. 8 §47, footnote 54 (p. 355 in the Wengrov English translation). We became aware of the remaining five entries from various searches of our own. After finding those five, we learned that various reference works also record them. We catalog those references below.

MAM's note at 1 Kgs. 7:37 reports that Aleppo has the later meteg, while Leningrad has the silluq alone. MAM's body text has the meteg after silluq, following Aleppo, as is MAM's usual policy (φ4).

At 1 Kgs. 14:14, UXLC acquired a meteg after the silluq through Daniel Holman's change proposal 2022.08.31-17.

Below we catalog how these seven cases are or are not recorded in works by Breuer and Dotan.

bcv Breuer Dotan
1 Sam. 17:5 DM BHL AppA
1 Kgs. 7:37 CoS ✗
1 Kgs. 14:14 DM ✗
Ps. 60:10 DM BHL body
Ps. 70:2 DM BHL body
Ps. 72:15 DM BHL body
Job 4:12 ✗ BHL body

The abbreviations and codes in the first table are decoded below:

scholar code decoding
Breuer DM Da'at Miqra
Breuer CoS The Cantillation of Scripture
Dotan BHL Biblia Hebraica Leningradensia
Dotan ... AppA ... Appendix A
Dotan ... body ... body, i.e. non-Appendix text

Further notes on the first table:

  • The gray ✗ in Dotan's column marks BHL's expected omission at 1 Kgs. 7:37: Aleppo has the meteg after the silluq, while Leningrad has the silluq alone. BHL follows Leningrad, so its omission of the meteg is expected.
  • The red ✗ in Dotan's column marks BHL's omission at 1 Kgs. 14:14. BHL's body has only the silluq, and Appendix A has no entry. I regard that combined omission as an error.
  • The red ✗ in Breuer's column marks the absence of Job 4:12 from both Da'at Miqra and CoS. The omission may be intentional because the Aleppo and Leningrad codices agree there, so there might seem to be nothing to note. But Koren has the silluq alone, and the Second Rabbinic Bible (the Venice Mikra'ot Gedolot of 1524–25) appears to have the silluq alone. Koren would probably not be noted in either work, but Breuer typically notes the Second Rabbinic Bible with his sigil ד (dalet).

φ1 — Stroke angles

In this document, we ignore the vexing set of angles, some quite far from the vertical, that both meteg and silluq can take on, both within a single manuscript and across manuscripts.

φ2 — A distinct form for silluq

One book whose typography distinguishes silluq from meteg is the 2005 revised edition of The Torah: A Modern Commentary (W. Gunther Plaut, original editor; David E. S. Stein, revised-edition editor). There are thousands of examples that could be used, but let's use its version of the last word of Num. 23:26 (letters אעשה), because in this word both the silluq and the meteg appear next to a segol, providing an obvious visual yardstick:

φ3 — Other accents with a similar stroke

In this document, we set aside the broader set of accents that a similar stroke can represent: merkha, mayela, tipeḥa, and tarḥa. In prose verses, Yeivin, ITM §210, describes a secondary accent with the form of tipeḥa in the word that has silluq; §216 calls the corresponding accent mayela. Breuer, CoS, ch. 11 §80, records secondary tarḥa or merkha in the word that has silluq in poetic verses. The additional accents in those examples precede silluq, so they are outside this document's post-silluq scope.

φ4 — MAM's use of Aleppo

MAM diverges from Aleppo only when a specific editorial policy requires a different form or, in a rare case, when Aleppo is fairly clearly erroneous or fairly clearly outside the manuscript tradition of which Aleppo is generally the greatest example. Because meteg after silluq is so rare, such a judgment is difficult here, so it makes sense that MAM follows Aleppo in the two of our seven cases in which Aleppo has meteg after silluq: 1 Kgs. 7:37 and Job 4:12.
